pr_body:
Plugin downloads can sometimes take unexpectedly
long because of slow random number generation on certain
operating system versions, e.g. Debian based OS
distros with kernels older than 5.6. This PR adds
a warning message for users explaining why plugin
installation from remote URLs is taking unexpectedly long.

Closes #80480
pr_comments: Hi @grcevski, I've created a changelog YAML for you.

comments:
Hi @PMickael, this looks like an environmental issue on your installation. It seems like the java plugin installation process is stuck waiting on /dev/random on your system to generate random numbers. Sometimes this can be very slow as the system will wait for sufficient entropy to build up. I'd have to say 10-15 minutes is extremely long, but it definitely is some sort of a system issue. As you can see from the stack traces the plugin installer is waiting on the Native OS PRNG (Pseudo Random Number Generator) to respond.

This stackoverflow post has few suggestions on how to improve entropy or switch to a less secure random generator: https://stackoverflow.com/questions/137212/how-to-deal-with-a-slow-securerandom-generator

@grcevski this is a recurring problem that users find hard to debug:

- this report
- three users reporting this in https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/issues/68419
- https://discuss.elastic.co/t/elasticsearch-plugin-install-plugin-hangs/277732
- perhaps https://discuss.elastic.co/t/elasticsearch-plugin-install-repository-gcs-is-stuck/270537

Although the fundamental problem is environmental, it's far from obvious from the tool behaviour and so it basically looks like a bug. I think we should do more to help users understand why the tool is waiting and guide them towards investigating the problem in their environment. I'm reopening this for now to continue the conversation.
That's not the case @PMickael, Nikola's [previous message](https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/issues/80480#issuecomment-1035105937) describes the problem you're facing.
Thanks for those pointers, I didn't realize this is more common than a single instance. I'll investigate this in more depth.

Like said [here](https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/issues/68419#issuecomment-1035997900) it seems that this issue, at least on Ubuntu, is because Elasticsearch waits for a random string from `/dev/random` instead of `/dev/urandom`.

@DaveCTurner do you have any news on that? I experienced the issue again now. Note that this problem makes difficult to roll out Elasticsearch version upgrades because when you upgrade you have to remove and then re-install every plugin. With this issue this takes a lot of time while Elasticsearch is down.

It's fundamentally a system config issue @mmenozzi. On a properly configured system it should be possible to run `dd if=/dev/random of=/dev/null bs=1024 count=1 iflag=fullblock` in minimal time. If this command blocks then that's a problem you need to address. This isn't really the place to debug your system config, but hopefully it helps to note that Linux can gather entropy from numerous sources (e.g. the hardware RNG built into most modern CPUs) if configured properly. Try looking for things like `rng-tools`.
Anyway if someone here has the same issue I solved it by just installing `haveged` (`apt install haveged`). The plugin installation is much quicker now.
Thanks for the update @mmenozzi. Sorry about the delay, I was away until yesterday. I'll look into this more soon for completeness.

I was able to reproduce the problem with an older Ubuntu kernel (5.4 in my case). The debian 10 uses even older version, so I'm guessing this is going to be a similar issue there. On remote systems there simply isn't enough entropy from mouse or keyboard interaction for the older /dev/random to produce enough data and it simply blocks when we try to get a random number. I confirmed that switching to /dev/urandom resolves the issue, as well as the suggested solution by @mmenozzi to install haveged.

Haveged is already integrated in any kernel including and after 5.6 and those work very fast.

I think we should add a timer around the verify signature call in our InstallPluginCommand and inform the users that this is taking unreasonably long and it could be an insufficient entropy problem with random numbers generation, along with providing guidance on how to resolve the system issue. @DaveCTurner does this work, or you had a different approach in mind?

> does this work, or you had a different approach in mind?

That sounds perfect to me.

review_comments: Why not have this timer be local to computeSignatureForDownload?

The main reason I split it this way is to be able to mock computeSignatureForDownload, but I really like your suggestion, there's no reason to pollute the mainline of that code with the timer block. I'll extract into a method that signifies that we are wrapping with a timer.
